subject: Public health
summary: Key principles for preventing disease in East African hospitals: sanitation, vaccination, nutrition, surveillance, and rapid response. Clinicians must integrate public health into bedside care and ward management.

sections.p: Public health focuses on population health, disease prevention, and health promotion. In low‑resource settings, it is essential for reducing preventable admissions and improving outcomes.
b: Disease burden driven by sanitation, nutrition, and infectious agents
Health systems rely on surveillance, vaccination, and basic hygiene

sections.h: Features of the Public Health System
sections.p: A functional public health system includes surveillance, vaccination programmes, water and sanitation, nutrition, and health education.
b: Surveillance: case reporting, trend analysis
Vaccination: routine and outbreak control
Water & sanitation: safe drinking water, latrine coverage
Nutrition: iron‑deficiency prevention, complementary feeding

sections.h: Transmission and Life Cycle of Key Preventable Diseases
sections.p: Many common infections spread via contaminated water, food, or vectors. Understanding their life cycles guides control measures.
b: Water‑borne: cholera, typhoid
Food‑borne: hepatitis A, E
Vector‑borne: malaria, dengue

Positive guides antimalarial therapy

sections.p: Public health failures lead to outbreaks of diarrhoea, typhoid, malaria, and nutritional deficiencies.
b: Diarrhoeal disease: high morbidity in children
Typhoid fever: fever, abdominal pain, rose spots

b: History of water source, sanitation
Physical signs: dehydration, pallor

Positive confirms malaria

b: Antibiotics for bacterial infections
ORS for dehydration
Antimalarials for confirmed malaria

Avoids resistance by full course

sections.p: Clinicians must link bedside findings to public health interventions.
b: Ask about water source in diarrhoea
Check vaccination status in febrile illness
Advise iron supplementation in anaemic children

faq.q: What is the most common preventable cause of hospital admissions in Kenya?
faq.a: Diarrhoeal disease due to poor sanitation and unsafe water.

faq.q: Which vaccine is essential for children in East Africa?
faq.a: Oral cholera vaccine and routine immunisations (BCG, measles, polio).

faq.q: How do you manage a child with suspected iron‑deficiency anaemia?
faq.a: Give oral iron supplements, counsel on iron‑rich diet, and investigate for ongoing blood loss.

exam: A 5‑year‑old presents with fever and abdominal pain; stool culture is negative. What is the next step? — Consider typhoid; repeat culture or use Widal test; start empiric antibiotics if high suspicion.
A patient with suspected malaria has a negative rapid test but high clinical suspicion. What do you do? — Repeat test, consider microscopy, treat empirically if severe.
A ward has an outbreak of diarrhoea. What public health measure should you implement first? — Ensure safe drinking water, promote hand hygiene, isolate cases.
Why is iron supplementation avoided in a patient with haemoglobinuria? — Risk of worsening renal damage; investigate underlying cause first.
What is the key difference between typhoid fever and malaria on physical exam? — Typhoid may have rose spots; malaria often has splenomegaly.
When is oral cholera vaccine indicated? — During cholera outbreaks or in high‑risk communities.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect a focused history and perform a systematic exam to identify key public‑health clues and rule out mimics.
b: History: source of drinking water, sanitation facilities, recent travel, food intake, vaccination status, exposure to animals, recent fever or rash, family history of TB or malaria.

Examination: inspect skin for pallor, jaundice, rashes; check conjunctiva for pallor or icterus; auscultate lungs for wheeze or crackles; palpate abdomen for tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites (shifting dullness).
Check capillary refill (<2 s normal); assess dehydration by skin turgor, sunken eyes, dry mucosa; note any fever spikes or night sweats.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use point‑of‑care tests and simple labs to confirm etiology, gauge severity, and guide treatment, especially where resources are limited.

t.b: Detects Plasmodium antigens; positive confirms malaria, negative with high clinical suspicion warrants microscopy or repeat test.
Assesses anemia; <10 g/dL in children suggests iron deficiency or chronic disease.
Evaluates dehydration severity; clear urine and normal skin turgor indicate mild dehydration.
Any growth confirms typhoid; guides antibiotic choice.
Positive proteinuria may indicate renal involvement or severe malaria.
Shows infiltrates or effusion; helps differentiate pneumonia from TB.

t.a: Mantoux test or interferon‑γ release assay
t.b: Positive indicates latent TB; negative in immunocompromised may miss infection.
Positive confirms viral gastroenteritis; guides supportive care.
Hyperglycemia can worsen infection outcomes; normal range 70‑110 mg/dL.
Leukocytosis with left shift suggests bacterial infection; eosinophilia may hint at parasitic disease.

sections.p: Apply standard classification systems to stratify patients and decide management pathways.
b: Diarrhoea: WHO danger signs – lethargy, vomiting, inability to drink, sunken eyes, skin pinch >2 s.

sections.p: Differentiate common mimics using key clinical and investigative clues.

t.b: Fever, abdominal pain, rose spots; confirm with stool culture or Widal test.
Sudden fever spikes, chills, anemia; confirm with RDT or microscopy.
Rapid, profuse watery diarrhoea, no blood; confirm with stool culture for Vibrio cholerae.
Fever, vomiting, watery stool, no blood; supportive care only.
Weight‑for‑height Z < ‑3, MUAC < 115 mm, or bilateral pitting oedema; requires therapeutic feeding.

sections.p: A systematic approach ensures that immediate threats are addressed, definitive therapy is started, and the patient is monitored for response and complications, with clear triggers for escalation or referral.
b: 1. Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation; give high‑flow oxygen if hypoxic and start IV access.
2. Re‑hydrate with oral rehydration solution; if capillary refill >2 seconds or shock signs, give rapid IV isotonic fluids.
3. Start empiric antimicrobial therapy based on likely pathogen (e.g., fluoroquinolone for suspected typhoid, artemisinin‑based combination for confirmed malaria).
4. Initiate disease‑specific interventions: ORS for diarrhoea, antipyretics for fever, vitamin A for measles, iron supplementation only after ruling out haemoglobinuria.
5. Monitor vitals, urine output, stool frequency, and hydration status every hour initially; repeat malaria test if clinical suspicion persists.
6. Escalate to referral if: persistent shock despite fluids, severe dehydration with altered mental status, failure to defervesce after 48 h, or need for intensive care.
7. Document and report case to local surveillance system within 24 h; trigger community‑level interventions (water safety, vaccination campaigns).

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding adverse effects and interactions prevents iatrogenic harm and guides prompt management.
b: Fluoroquinolones: tendinitis, QT prolongation; avoid in patients on anti‑arrhythmics or with known cardiac conduction disease.
Artemisinin‑based combos: rare hepatotoxicity; check baseline transaminases if pre‑existing liver disease.
Macrolides (azithromycin): gastrointestinal upset, possible drug‑drug interaction with protease inhibitors; monitor for diarrhoea.
Cotrimoxazole (for opportunistic infections): can cause severe neutropenia; stop if white cell count falls below 1 × 10⁹/L.
Iron salts: cause constipation and oxidative stress; discontinue if haemoglobinuria or infection worsens.

t.b: Obtain ECG; if QT >500 ms, switch to non‑QT‑prolonging antibiotic.
If transaminases rise >5 × ULN, pause antimalarial and reassess.
Hold cotrimoxazole, give granulocyte colony‑stimulating factor if severe.

sections.p: Early recognition of complications guides timely referral and prevents mortality.
b: Severe dehydration: persistent tachycardia, hypotension, capillary refill >2 seconds after two fluid boluses – refer for intensive care.
Acute kidney injury: oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/h, rising creatinine – initiate renal monitoring and consider referral.
Septic shock: lactate >2 mmol/L, mental status change – start vasopressors and transfer.
Severe anaemia (Hb <5 g/dL) from malaria or typhoid – arrange blood transfusion.
Intestinal perforation in typhoid – urgent surgical assessment.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and contextual factors modify presentation, test performance, and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV: lower CD4 reduces febrile response; opportunistic infections mimic malaria; prefer rapid antigen tests with higher sensitivity.
TB co‑infection: may cause chronic fever, anemia; avoid BCG revaccination in active disease.
Severe acute malnutrition: weight‑for‑height Z‑score < ‑3, MUAC < 115 mm, or bilateral pitting oedema – fluid resuscitation must be cautious, use low‑volume ORS.
Pregnancy: avoid tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones; use azithromycin for typhoid, ACTs safe in second/third trimester.
Diabetes: hyperglycaemia worsens infection outcomes; monitor glucose and adjust insulin during infection.
Alcohol use: impairs liver metabolism of antimalarials; watch for hepatotoxicity.
Renal failure: dose‑adjust antibiotics cleared renally; prefer ceftriaxone over renally cleared drugs.
Elderly: blunted fever, higher risk of dehydration; lower fluid thresholds, monitor electrolytes closely.

sections.p: Tailoring interventions to vulnerable populations maximises benefit while minimising harm.
b: Children <5 years: use weight‑based ACTs, give zinc with ORS, monitor for rapid dehydration; avoid ibuprofen if dehydration present.
Pregnant women: give ACTs (artesunate‑lumefantrine) after first trimester, azithromycin for typhoid, iron only after confirming no haemoglobinuria.
Elderly: start fluids slower, watch for heart failure, choose antibiotics with low nephrotoxicity.
People with HIV: screen for CD4, use cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, consider drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals.
Low‑resource settings: rely on clinical algorithms, use point‑of‑care malaria RDTs, treat presumptively when labs unavailable, reinforce community water safety.

t.b: When microscopy unavailable, use RDTs for malaria; if negative but high suspicion, repeat after 24 h.
If outbreak of diarrhoea, first implement chlorination of water sources and hand‑washing stations.

facts: Severe acute malnutrition: weight‑for‑height Z‑score <‑3, MUAC <115 mm, or bilateral pitting oedema.
Stool culture positive for Salmonella Typhi: any growth confirms diagnosis.
BCG vaccine is not given to children >5 years with active pulmonary TB; it is for infants to prevent severe TB forms.
Capillary refill >2 seconds indicates severe dehydration; IV fluids are required before ORS.
Oral rehydration solution (ORS) composition: 75 mmol/L sodium, 75 mmol/L glucose, osmolarity ≤300 mOsm/L.
Typhoid fever incubation: 7‑14 days; classic rose spots appear on trunk in 10‑30% of cases.
Cholera oral vaccine (Euvichol‑Plus) is indicated for travelers to endemic areas and during outbreaks in high‑risk populations.
Standard TB treatment regimen (RIPE): Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol for 2 months intensive phase.
WHO growth reference: MUAC 115‑125 mm indicates moderate acute malnutrition.
Vector‑borne malaria: rapid diagnostic test (RDT) sensitivity >95% for P. falciparum when parasite density >100/µL.

mnemonics.t: Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol – first‑line drugs for active TB.
Vaccination, Infrastructure, Training, Access, Legislation – core components of a functional public health system.

vivas.q: What public‑health action is essential after diagnosing a child with pulmonary TB?
vivas.a: Report to the national TB programme, initiate contact tracing of household members, and start directly observed therapy (DOT) for the child.

vivas.q: What proportion of the global chronic disease burden is preventable by optimal dietary habits?
vivas.a: Approximately 20‑30% of non‑communicable disease burden can be averted through improved diet.

vivas.q: Which age‑related pattern is seen for pediatric enteric viral pathogens?
vivas.a: Rotavirus peaks at 6‑24 months, while norovirus (calicivirus) is more common after 2 years and in older children.

vivas.q: Antigenic shift in influenza is most often driven by:
vivas.a: Reassortment of gene segments between human and animal (avian or swine) influenza viruses.

vivas.q: Calicivirus outbreaks in daycare centers differ from rotavirus outbreaks by:
vivas.a: Shorter incubation (12‑48 h) and a higher proportion of vomiting than diarrhoea.

vivas.q: Which healthcare tier is used when a village‑level immunisation drive is launched for measles?
vivas.a: Primary health care level – community health workers and health‑facility nurses delivering vaccines.

vivas.q: What is the likely consequence of bypassing local leadership during community entry?
vivas.a: Loss of community trust, reduced participation, and possible resistance to interventions.

vivas.q: A 4‑year‑old presents with abrupt fever, severe sore throat, inspiratory stridor progressing rapidly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: Acute epiglottitis; requires immediate airway protection and IV antibiotics.

vivas.q: Why is iron supplementation avoided in a patient with haemoglobinuria?
vivas.a: Because excess iron can promote bacterial growth and worsen haemolysis; also risk of oxidative injury.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate typhoid fever from malaria on physical exam?
vivas.a: Typhoid often shows relative bradycardia and rose spots; malaria may have splenomegaly and periodic chills.

vivas.q: When is oral cholera vaccine indicated?
vivas.a: During cholera outbreaks, for travelers to endemic areas, and in high‑risk populations lacking safe water.

vivas.q: What bedside test cannot reliably distinguish between bacterial and viral diarrhoea?
vivas.a: Stool microscopy for leukocytes; it has low specificity in low‑resource settings.

vivas.q: What is the first public‑health measure in a ward outbreak of diarrhoea?
vivas.a: Ensure safe water and reinforce hand‑washing; isolate cases and provide ORS.

vivas.q: Why is capillary refill >2 seconds a trigger for IV fluids in severe dehydration?
vivas.a: It indicates poor peripheral perfusion; oral rehydration alone may be insufficient.

vivas.q: What is the role of surveillance in low‑resource public‑health systems?
vivas.a: Early detection of outbreaks, trend analysis, and guiding resource allocation for interventions.

vivas.q: Explain one reason why BCG is not given to a 7‑year‑old with active pulmonary TB.
vivas.a: BCG is a prophylactic vaccine; it does not treat active disease and offers limited benefit after exposure.

vivas.q: What is the key component of nutrition‑focused public‑health interventions for children under five?
vivas.a: Promotion of exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months and timely complementary feeding with micronutrient‑rich foods.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection modify the presentation of TB in the community?
vivas.a: Higher rates of extrapulmonary TB, atypical chest X‑ray, and faster progression to severe disease.

mcqs.q: Which of the following best describes antigenic shift in influenza viruses?
o: Reassortment of whole genome segments between species
mcqs.e: Shift occurs when two different influenza viruses infect the same cell and exchange gene segments, creating a novel subtype.

mcqs.q: In a community outbreak of cholera, which intervention provides the greatest immediate reduction in transmission?
o: Provision of safe drinking water and chlorination
mcqs.e: Safe water and chlorination stop the fecal‑oral spread instantly; vaccines take weeks to confer immunity.

mcqs.q: A 7‑year‑old with confirmed pulmonary TB is started on treatment. Which statement is correct regarding BCG vaccination?
o: BCG is contraindicated in active disease
Give BCG now to boost immunity
BCG should be given after treatment completion
BCG is optional in school‑aged children
mcqs.e: BCG is a preventive vaccine; it is not indicated for children with active TB.

mcqs.q: Which sign differentiates ascites from pleural effusion on physical exam?
mcqs.e: Shifting dullness is specific for fluid in the abdomen; pleural effusion shows dullness that does not shift with position.

mcqs.q: During a measles outbreak, which level of the health system is primarily responsible for vaccine delivery?
mcqs.e: Primary health care facilities and community health workers conduct routine immunisation campaigns.

mcqs.q: A child with severe acute malnutrition presents with bilateral pitting oedema. Which classification applies?
mcqs.e: Presence of bilateral pitting oedema meets the WHO criteria for severe acute malnutrition regardless of anthropometry.

cases.v: A 2‑month‑old infant in a rural health centre develops watery diarrhoea, vomiting, and sunken eyes. Capillary refill is 3 seconds, and the infant is lethargic. No stool microscopy is available.

qs.q: What is the first line of rehydration?
qs.a: Begin intravenous isotonic fluid bolus (20 mL/kg) because capillary refill >2 seconds indicates severe dehydration.

qs.q: If IV access cannot be obtained, what is the next best option?
qs.a: Administer oral rehydration solution using a nasogastric tube if the infant can tolerate it.

qs.q: Which public‑health intervention will prevent future cases in this community?
qs.a: Improve water safety through chlorination and promote hand‑washing with soap at household level.

mistakes: Omitting bilateral pitting oedema as a criterion for severe acute malnutrition.
Stating a numeric CFU cut‑off for Salmonella Typhi stool culture; any growth is diagnostic.
Recommending BCG vaccination for a child with active pulmonary TB.
Using capillary refill >2 seconds as a reason to give only ORS in severe dehydration.
Confusing antigenic drift with antigenic shift in influenza.
Assuming a negative malaria RDT rules out malaria without considering parasite density.
Neglecting to report a confirmed TB case to the national programme.
Failing to consider HIV co‑infection when evaluating atypical TB presentations.
